prompt: `unbounded.go` worked under an open-file limit of 1,024 and lost 752 of 1,000 jobs under 256. What does that say about the program?
hint: Nothing in the program changed between the two runs.

choices.text: Goroutines fail when more than 256 exist
choices.why: Goroutines have no such limit; the files did. The same thousand goroutines succeeded under 1,024.

choices.text: Only the environment limited it, by accident
choices.why: Right. It held as many files as it had goroutines, and the limit it met was whoever ran it.

choices.text: `/etc/hostname` cannot be opened twice
choices.why: A file can be opened by any number of goroutines; the run under 1,024 opened it a thousand times.

choices.text: The mutex serialised the jobs and made them time out
choices.why: The mutex guards only the two counters, and nothing in the program has a timeout.

prompt: In `pool.go`, who closes `results`, and why not a worker?
hint: What does a worker not know when its own loop ends?

choices.text: The producer, right after it has sent the last job
choices.why: Workers may still be running jobs and sending results then; closing would make their sends panic.

choices.text: Each worker, at the moment its own loop ends
choices.why: Fifty closes of one channel: the second one panics.

choices.text: Whoever waits on `wg.Wait`
choices.why: Right. A worker knows its own loop ended, not whether the other forty-nine have.

choices.text: `main`, after it has read the last result
choices.why: `main` cannot know which result is the last until the channel is closed; that is what it waits for.

prompt: Somebody deletes `close(jobs)` from `pool.go`'s producer. What happens?
hint: Follow a worker's `for range jobs` after the last job.

choices.text: The workers wait for more jobs, and so does `main`
choices.why: Right. The chain of closes breaks at its first link, and every goroutine downstream waits.

choices.text: The workers stop after the last job on their own
choices.why: A `for range` over a channel ends only when the channel is closed.

choices.text: The program panics on the next send to `jobs`
choices.why: Nothing sends after the last job, and sending on an open channel never panics.

choices.text: The jobs run twice
choices.why: Each value on a channel is received once; nothing repeats it.

prompt: `pool.go` runs 1,000 jobs of 50 ms each on 50 workers. If each worker spends almost all its time in jobs, about how many milliseconds should the whole run take?
hint: How many rounds of fifty, and how long is a round?

prompt: `size cpu` took 2.039 s with one worker and 572 ms with four, and eight workers were no real improvement. Why not?
hint: How many goroutines may compute at once on this machine?

choices.text: The channel `jobs` can feed only four workers
choices.why: Any number of workers may receive from one channel; sixteen did.

choices.text: Four processors, so four goroutines compute at a time
choices.why: Right. A fifth worker only takes turns with the others.

choices.text: The jobs share memory and slow each other down
choices.why: `compute` shares nothing except writing its result to `sink`; the limit is processors.

choices.text: The garbage collector pauses the extra workers while they compute
choices.why: `compute` allocates nothing, so the collector has no part in this.

prompt: Why did `size wait` keep getting faster all the way to 64 workers, while `size cpu` stopped at four?
hint: What does a sleeping worker need?

choices.text: Sleeping jobs are shorter than computing ones
choices.why: Twenty against about thirty milliseconds is a small difference; it does not explain a curve that keeps falling.

choices.text: `time.Sleep` runs on a separate processor
choices.why: There is no such processor. A sleeping goroutine simply needs none.

choices.text: A waiting worker needs no processor
choices.why: Right, so the processor count sets no ceiling; the thing waited on does.

choices.text: Go raises `GOMAXPROCS` when goroutines sleep
choices.why: `GOMAXPROCS` stays at four throughout; it is a setting, not something the runtime raises.

prompt: Each job calls a partner's API, which allows 10 requests at a time from your account and refuses the rest. The jobs mostly wait. What pool size does the section's reasoning give?
hint: For waiting work, the ceiling is on the other end.

choices.text: `runtime.GOMAXPROCS(0)`, as for computing work
choices.why: That rule is for jobs that compute. These wait, and the partner sets the limit.

choices.text: As many as there are jobs
choices.why: Then most requests would be refused, which is `unbounded.go` against an API.

choices.text: 64, since that was fastest in `size wait`
choices.why: That measured a sleep, which anyone can share. The partner's API cannot be shared that way.

choices.text: At most 10, less whatever else uses that account
choices.why: Right. The limit of the thing on the other end, minus its other users.

prompt: Order the `size cpu` runs from the fastest to the slowest, as the capture printed them.
hint: Past four workers the numbers are close: read them.

prompt: In `semaphore.go`, what does a send on `sem` mean?

choices.text: Taking a place, waiting if none is free
choices.why: Right. The deferred receive gives the place back when the job ends.

choices.text: Handing the next job to one of the waiting workers
choices.why: There are no workers here; the empty struct carries nothing to anybody.

choices.text: Reporting to `main` that a job has failed
choices.why: Failures are counted with `failed.Add(1)`; the send happens before the job even starts.

choices.text: Closing a file
choices.why: `f.Close()` closes the file, deferred inside `job`.

prompt: A colleague moves `sem <- struct{}{}` from the loop to the first line inside the goroutine. Files stay under the limit. What changes?
hint: When does the loop start the thousandth goroutine now?

choices.text: Nothing at all
choices.why: The work is still limited, but the number of goroutines no longer is.

choices.text: Jobs fail with too many open files again
choices.why: The place is still taken before `os.Open`, so at most fifty files are open.

choices.text: 1,000 goroutines exist at once; fifty of them work
choices.why: Right. Acquiring in the loop is what kept the goroutine count bounded too.

choices.text: The program deadlocks on the fifty-first send to `sem`
choices.why: The fifty-first goroutine waits until a place frees, and places keep freeing as jobs end.

prompt: Match each situation with the shape the section suggests for it.
hint: One shape keeps fixed goroutines; the other one per job.

pairs.left: a stream of jobs from a queue that never ends
a known list of jobs, each a function call
pairs.right: a buffered channel as a semaphore

pairs.left: jobs that compute and nothing else

right_distractors: one goroutine per job with no limit

prompt: The element type of `sem` takes no memory, because the channel only counts: it is the empty ___.
A pool of 4 workers resizes photos, which is pure computation, on a machine with 4 processors. Someone raises it to 40 to 'go faster'. What should they expect, by the lesson's measurements?

choices.text: About ten times faster
choices.why: Ten times the workers is not ten times the processors; four still compute at a time.

choices.text: About the same time, give or take the noise between runs
choices.why: Right: 572, 543 and 560 ms for 4, 8 and 16 workers.

choices.text: Failures with too many open files
choices.why: Pure computation opens nothing; that failure belonged to jobs holding files.

choices.text: A deadlock, because 40 exceeds `GOMAXPROCS`
choices.why: Sixteen workers ran on four processors without trouble; extra workers take turns.

prompt: Which of these does a worker pool limit? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think of `pool.go` with a thousand jobs and fifty workers.

choices.text: How many jobs are in progress at once
choices.why: Yes, at most one per worker.

choices.text: How many goroutines do the work
choices.why: Yes, the workers are a fixed number.

choices.text: How many jobs may wait in the queue
choices.why: The producer can offer any number; it waits on the send, but the list behind it is unbounded.

choices.text: How long each job may take
choices.why: Nothing in the pool times a job; that needs a deadline, lesson 10.

prompt: Which line in `pool.go` decides how many files may be open at once?

choices.text: `f, err := os.Open("/etc/hostname")`
choices.why: That opens one file per job; how many jobs run at once is decided elsewhere.

choices.text: `const workers = 50`
choices.why: Right: one job per worker, one file per job.

choices.text: `jobs := make(chan int)`
choices.why: An unbuffered channel holds no jobs; it only hands them over.

choices.text: `for i := range 1000`
choices.why: That is the number of jobs, not how many run together.

prompt: The shell command `ulimit ___` prints how many files a process started from that shell may have open at once.
`size wait` runs 64 jobs of 20 ms each. With 16 workers, how many rounds of jobs does the run take, if each worker always has a job ready?
